claims.claim: The effect of synaptic mutants on AIA responses was most evident at low diacetyl concentrations.
claims.source: This effect was most evident at low diacetyl concentrations, where the synaptic mutants substantially decreased the latency of the AIA response (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Inactivation of dense core vesicle release with an unc-31 mutation did not alter AIA reliability.
claims.source: Inactivation of dense core vesicle release with an unc-31 mutation did not alter AIA reliability, demonstrating specificity of the effect (Richmond, 2007) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and cited from Richmond, 2007.

claims.claim: Chemical synapses are net inhibitory onto AIA.
claims.source: Chemical synapses are thus net inhibitory onto AIA.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the increased reliability of AIA responses in synaptic transmission mutants.

claims.claim: In synaptic mutants, half of the AIA neurons responded to AWA::Chrimson within 1.2 s, a dramatic decrease in latency compared to wild type (>6 s).
claims.source: In the synaptic mutants, half of the AIA neurons responded to AWA::Chrimson within 1.2 s, a dramatic decrease in latency compared to wild type (>6 s) (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The AWA-to-AIA delay in synaptic mutants after AWA::Chrimson stimulation resembled the delay to high concentrations of diacetyl.
claims.source: The AWA-to-AIA delay in synaptic mutants after AWA::Chrimson stimulation resembled the delay to high concentrations of diacetyl (Figure 3F–G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3F–G.

claims.claim: Direct AWA responses to optogenetic stimulation did not increase in unc-13 synaptic mutants.
claims.source: Control experiments demonstrated that direct AWA responses to optogenetic stimulation did not increase in unc-13 synaptic mutants (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D.

claims.claim: Chemical synapses inhibit AIA interneurons primarily by decreasing the reliability of AIA's response at a given level of AWA activation.
claims.source: Chemical synapses thus inhibit AIA interneurons primarily by decreasing the reliability of AIA's response at a given level of AWA activation.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with synaptic transmission mutants.

claims.claim: Eighteen pairs of neurons form chemical synapses onto AIA, six of which are sensory neurons that use glutamate as a neurotransmitter.
claims.source: Eighteen pairs of neurons form chemical synapses onto AIA, six of which are sensory neurons that use glutamate as a neurotransmitter (White et al., 1986; Cook et al., 2019; Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is cited from White et al., 1986, Cook et al., 2019, and Serrano-Saiz et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Glutamate hyperpolarizes AIA, likely by activating glutamate-gated chloride channels.
claims.source: Glutamate hyperpolarizes AIA, likely by activating glutamate-gated chloride channels, so these glutamatergic sensory neurons are plausible sources of the synaptic inhibition of AIA (Chalasani et al., 2010; Shinkai et al., 2011; López-Cruz et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Chalasani et al., 2010, Shinkai et al., 2011, and López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Selective excision of eat-4 in four tax-4-expressing sensory neurons (AWC, ASE, ASK, and ASG) allowed AWA::Chrimson stimulation to evoke reliable AIA responses similar to those in unc-18 synaptic transmission mutants.
claims.source: Selective excision of eat-4 in four tax-4-expressing sensory neurons, AWC, ASE, ASK, and ASG, allowed AWA::Chrimson stimulation to evoke reliable AIA responses similar to those in unc-18 synaptic transmission mutants (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: No individual sensory pair accounted for the full effect of preventing glutamate release from AWC, ASE, ASK, and ASG together.
claims.source: No individual sensory pair accounted for the full effect of preventing glutamate release from AWC, ASE, ASK, and ASG together (Figure 4D–4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C), although a significant partial effect was observed upon inhibition of glutamate release from ASK alone (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4D–4H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C.

claims.claim: A significant partial effect was observed upon inhibition of glutamate release from ASK alone.
claims.source: No individual sensory pair accounted for the full effect of preventing glutamate release from AWC, ASE, ASK, and ASG together (Figure 4D–4H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and C), although a significant partial effect was observed upon inhibition of glutamate release from ASK alone (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: In two independent lines in which unc-18 was selectively rescued in ASE and AWC, AIA interneuron responses were restored to unreliable responses resembling wild type.
claims.source: As noted above, the unc-18 mutant has increased reliability of AIA responses to AWA::Chrimson stimulation, but in two independent lines in which unc-18 was selectively rescued in ASE and AWC, AIA interneuron responses were restored to unreliable responses resembling wild type (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Synaptic vesicle release from AWC and ASE is sufficient to inhibit AIA activation by AWA.
claims.source: Synaptic vesicle release from AWC and ASE is therefore sufficient to inhibit AIA activation by AWA.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the rescue experiments with unc-18 in AWC and ASE.

claims.claim: Multiple sensory neurons, including ASK and at least one of AWC and ASE, can release glutamate to inhibit AIA activation.
claims.source: In summary, multiple sensory neurons, including ASK and at least one of AWC and ASE, can release glutamate to inhibit AIA activation.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with cell-specific glutamate knockout and rescue.

claims.claim: Glutamatergic sensory neurons tonically inhibit AIA, and are inhibited when diacetyl is present to disinhibit AIA.
claims.source: To explain these results, we hypothesized that glutamatergic sensory neurons tonically inhibit AIA, and are inhibited when diacetyl is present to disinhibit AIA.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental results.

claims.claim: ASK and AWC are active at rest and inhibited by amino acids, pheromones, and certain odors.
claims.source: This hypothesis agrees with previous calcium imaging studies showing that ASK and AWC are active at rest and inhibited by amino acids, pheromones, and certain odors (Wakabayashi et al., 2009; Macosko et al., 2009; Zaslaver et al., 2015; Chalasani et al., 2007; Kato et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Wakabayashi et al., 2009, Macosko et al., 2009, Zaslaver et al., 2015, Chalasani et al., 2007, and Kato et al., 2014.

claims.claim: ASK and AWC were inhibited by the addition of 1.15 µM diacetyl.
claims.source: To extend this observation to diacetyl, we expressed the genetically-encoded calcium indicator GCaMP5A in ASK and AWC, and GCaMP3 in ASE, and determined that ASK and AWC were inhibited by the addition of 1.15 µM diacetyl, whereas ASE was activated by diacetyl at the same concentration (Figure 5A–5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A–5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: ASE was activated by 1.15 µM diacetyl.
claims.source: To extend this observation to diacetyl, we expressed the genetically-encoded calcium indicator GCaMP5A in ASK and AWC, and GCaMP3 in ASE, and determined that ASK and AWC were inhibited by the addition of 1.15 µM diacetyl, whereas ASE was activated by diacetyl at the same concentration (Figure 5A–5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A–5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: All sensory neuron responses to diacetyl were dose-dependent, with responses that were weaker (ASK) or absent (AWC, ASE) at 11.5 nM diacetyl.
claims.source: All responses were dose-dependent, with responses that were weaker (ASK) or absent (AWC, ASE) at 11.5 nM diacetyl (Figure 5A–5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C,E–G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A–5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C, E–G.

claims.claim: ASH did not respond to 1.15 µM diacetyl.
claims.source: ASH, another glutamatergic sensory neuron that forms chemical synapses onto AIA, did not respond to 1.15 µM diacetyl (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and H), demonstrating neuronal specificity of the response.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and H.

claims.claim: Diacetyl responses in ASK and AWC were unchanged in unc-18 synaptic transmission mutants.
claims.source: Diacetyl responses in ASK and AWC were unchanged in unc-18 synaptic transmission mutants, suggesting that these neurons detect diacetyl directly (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–J,L–M).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–J, L–M.

claims.claim: ASK and AWC detect diacetyl directly.
claims.source: Diacetyl responses in ASK and AWC were unchanged in unc-18 synaptic transmission mutants, suggesting that these neurons detect diacetyl directly (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I–J,L–M).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the unchanged responses in synaptic transmission mutants.

claims.claim: Diacetyl responses in ASE were eliminated in unc-18 mutants.
claims.source: By contrast, diacetyl responses in ASE were eliminated in unc-18 mutants, suggesting that ASE senses diacetyl indirectly via another sensory neuron (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1K.

claims.claim: ASE senses diacetyl indirectly via another sensory neuron.
claims.source: By contrast, diacetyl responses in ASE were eliminated in unc-18 mutants, suggesting that ASE senses diacetyl indirectly via another sensory neuron (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the eliminated responses in synaptic transmission mutants.

claims.claim: AWA was not the source of the diacetyl response in ASE.
claims.source: AWA was not the source of the diacetyl response in ASE, as the response was preserved in an odr-10 diacetyl receptor mutant (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1K.

claims.claim: Neither ASK, AWC, nor ASE showed a calcium response upon AWA::Chrimson stimulation.
claims.source: Neither ASK, AWC, nor ASE showed a calcium response upon AWA::Chrimson stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1N–O).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1N–O.

claims.claim: AIA responses are unreliable upon AWA::Chrimson stimulation, which activates only AWA.
claims.source: In summary, AIA responses are unreliable upon AWA::Chrimson stimulation, which activates only AWA; more reliable to 11.5 nM diacetyl, which activates AWA and inhibits ASK; and highly reliable to 1.15 µM diacetyl, which activates AWA and ASE and inhibits AWC and ASK, leading to disinhibition of AIA (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 1-5.

claims.claim: AIA responses are more reliable to 11.5 nM diacetyl, which activates AWA and inhibits ASK.
claims.source: In summary, AIA responses are unreliable upon AWA::Chrimson stimulation, which activates only AWA; more reliable to 11.5 nM diacetyl, which activates AWA and inhibits ASK; and highly reliable to 1.15 µM diacetyl, which activates AWA and ASE and inhibits AWC and ASK, leading to disinhibition of AIA (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 1-5.

claims.claim: AIA responses are highly reliable to 1.15 µM diacetyl, which activates AWA and ASE and inhibits AWC and ASK, leading to disinhibition of AIA.
claims.source: In summary, AIA responses are unreliable upon AWA::Chrimson stimulation, which activates only AWA; more reliable to 11.5 nM diacetyl, which activates AWA and inhibits ASK; and highly reliable to 1.15 µM diacetyl, which activates AWA and ASE and inhibits AWC and ASK, leading to disinhibition of AIA (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figures 1-5.

claims.claim: AWC was inhibited by 0.9 µM isoamyl alcohol.
claims.source: We found that AWC was also inhibited by 0.9 µM isoamyl alcohol, and that AWA was activated by isoamyl alcohol in a graded fashion at 0.9, 9, and 90 µM isoamyl alcohol (Figure 5F–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B,D–E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5F–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B, D–E.

claims.claim: AWA was activated by isoamyl alcohol in a graded fashion at 0.9, 9, and 90 µM isoamyl alcohol.
claims.source: We found that AWC was also inhibited by 0.9 µM isoamyl alcohol, and that AWA was activated by isoamyl alcohol in a graded fashion at 0.9, 9, and 90 µM isoamyl alcohol (Figure 5F–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B,D–E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5F–G and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B, D–E.

claims.claim: ASK was not inhibited by isoamyl alcohol at any tested concentration.
claims.source: ASK was not inhibited by isoamyl alcohol at any tested concentration (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C and F.

claims.claim: AIA calcium responses to isoamyl alcohol were unreliable at the lowest concentrations, but became more reliable, with a higher probability and a shorter latency, as isoamyl alcohol concentration increased.
claims.source: As with diacetyl, AIA calcium responses were unreliable at the lowest concentrations, but became more reliable, with a higher probability and a shorter latency, as isoamyl alcohol concentration increased (Figure 5I–K, Figure 5—figure supplement 3K).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5I–K and Figure 5—figure supplement 3K.

claims.claim: At all isoamyl alcohol concentrations, AWC responded first and AIA responded later, near the time of AWA activation.
claims.source: At all concentrations, AWC responded first and AIA responded later, near the time of AWA activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 3G–I).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 3G–I.

claims.claim: For diacetyl, AWA responded first and AIA responded later, near the time of ASK inhibition.
claims.source: Interestingly, a different pattern held for diacetyl, where AWA responded first and AIA responded later, near the time of ASK inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplements 2A–D and 3J).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplements 2A–D and 3J.

claims.claim: odr-7 mutants had unreliable AIA responses to isoamyl alcohol at all concentrations.
claims.source: odr-7 mutants had unreliable AIA responses to isoamyl alcohol at all concentrations (Figure 5I–5K, Figure 5—figure supplement 3K).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5I–5K and Figure 5—figure supplement 3K.

claims.claim: At 9 µM and 90 µM isoamyl alcohol, AIA responses were more reliable in the odr-7 and ceh-36 single mutants than in the odr-7 ceh-36 double mutants.
claims.source: At the higher concentrations of 9 µM and 90 µM isoamyl alcohol, AIA responses were more reliable in the odr-7 and ceh-36 single mutants than in the odr-7 ceh-36 double mutants, indicating that AWA and AWC are partly redundant for AIA activation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5J–K and Figure 5—figure supplement 3K.

claims.claim: AWA and AWC are partly redundant for AIA activation at higher isoamyl alcohol concentrations.
claims.source: At the higher concentrations of 9 µM and 90 µM isoamyl alcohol, AIA responses were more reliable in the odr-7 and ceh-36 single mutants than in the odr-7 ceh-36 double mutants, indicating that AWA and AWC are partly redundant for AIA activation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of single and double mutants.

claims.claim: At 0.9 µM isoamyl alcohol, all mutants had unreliable AIA responses, indicating that both AWA and AWC are independently required for AIA activation.
claims.source: At the lower concentration of 0.9 µM isoamyl alcohol, all mutants had unreliable AIA responses, indicating that both AWA and AWC are independently required for AIA activation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: E. coli OP50-conditioned medium activates AWA and ASE and inhibits AWC, ASK, and several other sensory neurons.
claims.source: Previous work has shown that the more complex food stimulus of Escherichia coli OP50-conditioned medium activates AWA and ASE and inhibits AWC, ASK, and several other sensory neurons (Zaslaver et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Zaslaver et al., 2015.

claims.claim: OP50-conditioned medium elicited reliable AIA calcium responses with similar latency and rise dynamics to those elicited by high concentrations of diacetyl or isoamyl alcohol.
claims.source: We found that OP50-conditioned medium elicited reliable AIA calcium responses with similar latency and rise dynamics to those elicited by high concentrations of diacetyl or isoamyl alcohol (Figure 5L, Figure 5—figure supplement 3L–M).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5L and Figure 5—figure supplement 3L–M.

claims.claim: All stimuli that evoked reliable AIA responses engaged multiple sensory neurons, including inhibition of at least one glutamatergic sensory neuron and the activation of AWA.
claims.source: All stimuli that evoked reliable AIA responses engaged multiple sensory neurons, including inhibition of at least one glutamatergic sensory neuron and the activation of AWA (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: AIA membrane potential was bistable, with one stable state near the resting potential of −80 mV and a second state near −20 mV.
claims.source: We found that AIA membrane potential was bistable, with one stable state near the resting potential of −80 mV and a second state near −20 mV (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: A rapid transition between the two stable states of AIA occurred with a low current injection threshold near 2–3 pA.
claims.source: A rapid transition between these two states occurred with a low current injection threshold near 2–3 pA, at which point the AIA membrane potential rose rapidly to −20 mV (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A–C.

claims.claim: Subsequent increases in stimulus intensity did not greatly increase AIA membrane potential beyond −20 mV.
claims.source: Subsequent increases in stimulus intensity did not greatly increase AIA membrane potential beyond −20 mV.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6A–C.

claims.claim: AIA bistability is associated with a region of high membrane resistance between −80 and −20 mV.
claims.source: Voltage-clamp recordings indicate that AIA bistability is associated with a region of high membrane resistance between −80 and −20 mV (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claims.claim: Simultaneous recordings of membrane potential and GCaMP fluorescence in AIA during current injections revealed GCaMP fluorescence levels that were also bistable and stereotyped.
claims.source: Simultaneous recordings of membrane potential and GCaMP fluorescence in AIA during current injections revealed GCaMP fluorescence levels that were also bistable and stereotyped, with increases that were correlated with the voltage transition from −80 to −20 mV (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: AIA performs a nonlinear rather than an additive computation at a biophysical level.
claims.source: Thus AIA performs a nonlinear rather than an additive computation at a biophysical level.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the bistable electrophysiological properties of AIA.

claims.claim: In the absence of food odor, glutamatergic sensory neurons release glutamate that activates glutamate-gated chloride channels on AIA.
claims.source: In the absence of food odor, glutamatergic sensory neurons release glutamate that activates glutamate-gated chloride channels on AIA (López-Cruz et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is part of the proposed model and is cited from López-Cruz et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The chloride current decreases AIA membrane resistance, preventing AIA activation via the AWA-AIA electrical synapse.
claims.source: The chloride current decreases AIA membrane resistance, preventing AIA activation via the AWA-AIA electrical synapse.
claims.evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: In the presence of food odor, glutamatergic sensory neurons are inhibited, the glutamate-gated chloride channels close, and AIA disinhibition and increased AIA resistance make it more sensitive to depolarizing inputs.
claims.source: In the presence of food odor, glutamatergic sensory neurons are inhibited, the glutamate-gated chloride channels close, and AIA disinhibition and increased AIA resistance make it more sensitive to depolarizing inputs.
claims.evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Food odors activate AWA, driving AWA depolarization and calcium action potentials.
claims.source: At the same time, food odors activate AWA, driving AWA depolarization and calcium action potentials (Liu et al., 2018), and transmission of this information through AWA-to-AIA gap junctions depolarizes AIA to the plateau potential of −20 mV.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Liu et al., 2018 and is part of the proposed model.

claims.claim: Transmission of information through AWA-to-AIA gap junctions depolarizes AIA to the plateau potential of −20 mV.
claims.source: At the same time, food odors activate AWA, driving AWA depolarization and calcium action potentials (Liu et al., 2018), and transmission of this information through AWA-to-AIA gap junctions depolarizes AIA to the plateau potential of −20 mV.
claims.evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: For both diacetyl and isoamyl alcohol, AIA activation lags behind the first sensory neuron to detect odor, matching the arrival of the second input.
claims.source: For both diacetyl and isoamyl alcohol, AIA activation lags behind the first sensory neuron to detect odor, matching the arrival of the second input.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 5—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claims.claim: At low odor levels, the inhibition of the glutamatergic sensory neurons reported by calcium imaging is graded and gradual.
claims.source: At low odor levels, the inhibition of the glutamatergic sensory neurons reported by calcium imaging is graded and gradual.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A–C.

claims.claim: The first AWA action potential lags behind stimulus onset by about a second.
claims.source: Similarly, the first AWA action potential lags behind stimulus onset by about a second (Liu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Liu et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The depolarized state of AIA resembles the plateau potentials first reported in C. elegans RMD motor neurons.
claims.source: The depolarized state resembles the plateau potentials first reported in C. elegans RMD motor neurons (Mellem et al., 2008) and subsequently observed in a number of other C. elegans neurons that have a high resistance regime between stable low and high voltage states (Liu et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Mellem et al., 2008 and Liu et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The intrinsic bistability of AIA creates a threshold nonlinearity that shapes the response to synaptic inputs.
claims.source: The intrinsic bistability of AIA creates a threshold nonlinearity that shapes the response to synaptic inputs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the bistable electrophysiological properties of AIA.

claims.claim: The synaptic inputs are predicted to increase depolarizing current (through AWA gap junctions) and to increase membrane resistance (by closing glutamate-gated chloride channels).
claims.source: The synaptic inputs are predicted to increase depolarizing current (through AWA gap junctions) and to increase membrane resistance (by closing glutamate-gated chloride channels), and therefore could have the multiplicative effect on voltage classically defined by Ohm's law.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and basic electrophysiological principles.

claims.claim: A preferential effect of AWA gap junctions on depolarizing current, and inhibitory chemical synapses on membrane resistance and shunting, provide a plausible mechanism for the AIA AND-gate.
claims.source: A preferential effect of AWA gap junctions on depolarizing current, and inhibitory chemical synapses on membrane resistance and shunting, provide a plausible mechanism for the AIA AND-gate.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The AND-gate is an established motif in transcriptional regulation.
claims.source: The AND-gate is an established motif in transcriptional regulation (Buchler et al., 2003), and bears similarity to the related concept of coincidence detection in neural circuits (Koch, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Buchler et al., 2003 and Koch, 1999.

claims.claim: The AND-gate computation is nonlinear and multiplicative.
claims.source: In contrast with computational models of neurons based on additive inputs onto the target neuron (Dayan and Abbott, 2001; McCulloch and Pitts, 1943), the AND-gate computation is nonlinear and multiplicative (Koch, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Koch, 1999, Dayan and Abbott, 2001, and McCulloch and Pitts, 1943.

claims.claim: The AND-gate computation may filter out environmental noise.
claims.source: In the context of AIA, this logical computation requires multiple sensory neurons to report the presence of an attractant, an integrative step that may filter out environmental noise.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the functional significance of the AND-gate.

claims.claim: Different combinations of sensory neurons can generate the disinhibition and excitation necessary for reliable AIA activation.
claims.source: Based on our results with diacetyl and isoamyl alcohol, it appears that different combinations of sensory neurons can generate the disinhibition and excitation necessary for reliable AIA activation.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with diacetyl and isoamyl alcohol.

claims.claim: AIB activity rises when odors such as isoamyl alcohol are removed, triggering aversive behaviors such as reversals and turns.
claims.source: AIB activity rises when odors such as isoamyl alcohol are removed, triggering aversive behaviors such as reversals and turns (Chalasani et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Chalasani et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Stimuli that drive AIA responses in over 90% of trials, drive AIB responses in only 57% of trials.
claims.source: The coupling of strong odor stimuli to AIB activity is less reliable than coupling to AIA: stimuli that drive AIA responses in over 90% of trials, drive AIB responses in only 57% of trials (Gordus et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Gordus et al., 2015.

claims.claim: AIB variability results from its integration of sensory input with the downstream motor state.
claims.source: At a circuit level, AIB variability results from its integration of sensory input with the downstream motor state (Gordus et al., 2015), and AIB activity is highly correlated with the activity of other neurons that drive reversals (Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Gordus et al., 2015 and Kato et al., 2015.

claims.claim: AIA receives three times as many synapses from sensory neurons as from interneurons.
claims.source: In the C. elegans wiring diagram, AIA receives three times as many synapses from sensory neurons as from interneurons, and AIB receives equal numbers of synapses from sensory neurons and interneurons, perhaps explaining why AIA activity is more closely coupled to sensory state, and less to motor state, than AIB (White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: This is cited from White et al., 1986.

claims.claim: AIB receives equal numbers of synapses from sensory neurons and interneurons.
claims.source: In the C. elegans wiring diagram, AIA receives three times as many synapses from sensory neurons as from interneurons, and AIB receives equal numbers of synapses from sensory neurons and interneurons, perhaps explaining why AIA activity is more closely coupled to sensory state, and less to motor state, than AIB (White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: This is cited from White et al., 1986.

claims.claim: AIA activity is more closely coupled to sensory state, and less to motor state, than AIB.
claims.source: In the C. elegans wiring diagram, AIA receives three times as many synapses from sensory neurons as from interneurons, and AIB receives equal numbers of synapses from sensory neurons and interneurons, perhaps explaining why AIA activity is more closely coupled to sensory state, and less to motor state, than AIB (White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the wiring diagram and the experimental findings.

claims.claim: AWA primarily excites AIA via an electrical synapse, in the context of chemical synapses from other neurons.
claims.source: As predicted by the wiring diagram, our results indicate that AWA primarily excites AIA via an electrical synapse, in the context of chemical synapses from other neurons.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the experiments with innexin mutants and synaptic transmission mutants.

claims.claim: Mixed chemical-electrical synapses are present in many escape circuits, including insect giant fibers, goldfish Mauthner cells, and the C. elegans backward command neurons.
claims.source: Mixed chemical-electrical synapses are present in many escape circuits, including insect giant fibers, goldfish Mauthner cells, and the C. elegans backward command neurons (Allen and Murphey, 2007; Phelan et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Allen and Murphey, 2007, Phelan et al., 2008, and Liu et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In escape circuits, the same cells form chemical and electrical synapses with each other to maximize speed and efficiency.
claims.source: In these escape circuits, the same cells form chemical and electrical synapses with each other to maximize speed and efficiency.
claims.evidence: This is general knowledge about escape circuits.

claims.claim: The combination of inhibitory chemical synapses, excitatory gap junctions, and intrinsic bistability could represent the core features of an AND-gate circuit motif in C. elegans.

results.result: AIA interneurons require coincident activation of AWA and inhibition of glutamatergic sensory neurons for reliable responses. Optogenetic activation of AWA alone produces unreliable AIA responses (56% activation, >6s delay), while diacetyl at increasing concentrations produces progressively more reliable responses by engaging both AWA activation and inhibition of glutamatergic neurons (ASK, AWC). This demonstrates AND-gate logic requiring multiple coordinated sensory inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C44 demonstrate through optogenetics that AWA activation alone is insufficient (56% response rate, >6s delay vs. >90% for high diacetyl). Claims C106-C108 systematically show dose-dependent reliability correlating with engagement of multiple sensory pathways. The AND-gate interpretation (C2, C7) is well-supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches including mutant analysis (C52-C53) showing AWA is necessary but not sufficient.

results.result: AWA activates AIA through gap junctions composed of innexin proteins UNC-7 and UNC-9, with preferentially anterograde information flow. Chemical synapses from AWA are not required, as demonstrated by tetanus toxin experiments and synaptic transmission mutants. The gap junction is functionally asymmetric: AWA stimulation robustly activates AIA, but AIA stimulation produces only weak AWA responses.
results.evaluation: Multiple lines of evidence converge: tetanus toxin in AWA (C56-C57), unc-13/unc-18 mutants (C58-C59), innexin double mutants (C61-C63), and genetic rescue (C64-C65) all support gap junction-mediated transmission. Asymmetry is demonstrated by bidirectional optogenetic experiments (C67-C68). The wiring diagram predictions (C54-C55) are validated experimentally. Controls are appropriate and the logic is sound.

results.result: Chemical synapses from glutamatergic sensory neurons (AWC, ASE, ASK, ASG) tonically inhibit AIA. Synaptic transmission mutants (unc-13, unc-18) show faster and more reliable AIA responses to both diacetyl and AWA optogenetic stimulation. Cell-specific glutamate knockout and rescue experiments identify multiple redundant glutamatergic inputs, with ASK showing partial effects and AWC/ASE together being sufficient for inhibition.
results.evaluation: The counterintuitive finding that synaptic mutants enhance AIA responses (C78-C79, C82) is well-controlled (C80, C84) and mechanistically explained through glutamatergic inhibition (C86-C87). Cell-specific manipulations using eat-4-FRT (C88-C90) and unc-18 rescue (C91-C92) provide strong evidence for redundant glutamatergic inhibition. The conclusion of net inhibitory effect (C81, C85) is well-supported by multiple independent approaches.

results.result: Multiple sensory neurons detect attractive odors with distinct response profiles: ASK and AWC are tonically active and inhibited by diacetyl and isoamyl alcohol, while ASE is activated by diacetyl. These responses are dose-dependent and, for ASK and AWC, occur independently of synaptic transmission, indicating direct odor detection. ASE's response to diacetyl requires synaptic input from other neurons.
results.evaluation: Calcium imaging data (C96-C97, C109-C111) directly demonstrate the response profiles. Dose-dependence is shown systematically (C98). The distinction between direct and indirect sensing is supported by appropriate controls using unc-18 mutants (C100-C103). The hypothesis about tonic inhibition (C94) is supported by prior literature (C95) and the current data. The experimental design appropriately uses multiple odor concentrations and genetic controls.

results.result: AIA exhibits bistable electrophysiological properties with stable states at approximately -80 mV and -20 mV, transitioning rapidly at a low current threshold of 2-3 pA. This bistability is associated with high membrane resistance between these states and creates a threshold nonlinearity. Simultaneous voltage and calcium recordings show that GCaMP responses are also bistable and correlate with the voltage transition.
results.evaluation: Direct electrophysiological recordings (C122-C124) provide clear evidence for bistability. Voltage-clamp experiments (C125) support the mechanism. Simultaneous voltage and calcium measurements (C126) validate that the calcium imaging reflects the underlying bistable voltage dynamics. The conclusion about nonlinear computation (C127, C137) follows logically from the bistable properties. The experimental approach is rigorous with appropriate controls.

results.result: AIA responses to isoamyl alcohol demonstrate combinatorial integration with dose-dependent reliability. At low concentrations (0.9 μM), both AWA and AWC are independently required. At higher concentrations (9-90 μM), AWA and AWC show partial redundancy. This demonstrates that different combinations of sensory neurons can generate reliable AIA activation depending on stimulus strength.
results.evaluation: The dose-dependent reliability (C112) is systematically demonstrated. Genetic analysis using odr-7 (AWA mutant) and ceh-36 (AWC mutant) single and double mutants (C115-C118) provides clear evidence for both independent requirement at low doses and partial redundancy at high doses. This supports the broader conclusion about combinatorial integration (C143). The experimental design appropriately tests multiple concentrations and genetic combinations.

results.result: The proposed model for AIA AND-gate function involves glutamate-gated chloride channels that decrease membrane resistance in the absence of odor, preventing AWA-mediated activation via gap junctions. In the presence of attractive odors, glutamatergic neurons are inhibited, chloride channels close, resistance increases, and AWA depolarization can drive AIA to its plateau potential through gap junctions.
results.evaluation: This is a mechanistic model (C128-C132, C138-C139) that integrates the experimental findings but includes speculative elements. While the model is consistent with the data (glutamatergic inhibition, gap junction transmission, bistability), direct evidence for the specific mechanism (chloride channel closure increasing resistance to enable gap junction transmission) is not provided. The model invokes Ohm's law (C138) appropriately but lacks direct measurement of resistance changes during odor stimulation or direct demonstration of shunting at gap junctions.

results.result: AIA is proposed to encode positive valence based on integrated sensory state. This interpretation is supported by AIA's role in integrating attractive and repulsive stimuli (copper-diacetyl interactions requiring ASH inhibition of AIA) and by the observation that sensory neurons contributing to AIA activation have roles distinct from their roles in chemotaxis behavior.
results.evaluation: The valence encoding interpretation (C8, C161) is speculative and based on inference rather than direct measurement of valence. Supporting evidence from copper-diacetyl interactions (C162-C163) is cited but not experimentally demonstrated in this study. The dissociation between chemotaxis requirements and AIA activation requirements (C164-C165) is noted but not systematically tested. While the interpretation is plausible and consistent with the data, it requires additional behavioral and functional experiments to be fully supported.

results.result: AWA calcium responses to diacetyl are concentration-dependent, with stronger responses at 115 nM than 11.5 nM, and rapid desensitization at 1.15 μM. Optogenetic activation of AWA with Chrimson produces responses comparable in magnitude to ≥115 nM diacetyl, requires retinal and transgene expression, and shows minimal desensitization over 10 seconds.
results.evaluation: The concentration-dependence of AWA responses (C27-C29) is clearly demonstrated in Figure 1A,C and supported by prior work (Larsch et al., 2015). The optogenetic characterization (C32-C35) includes appropriate controls for retinal and transgene requirements (C34) and comparison to odor responses (C35). The data support the conclusion that optogenetic stimulation produces physiologically relevant AWA activation levels.

results.result: AIA calcium responses to diacetyl show stable baseline fluorescence, dose-dependent probability and latency (nearly all neurons respond to high concentrations with ~1s delay; lower probability and ~2s delay at 11.5 nM), and trial-to-trial variability in latency but not magnitude. Response latencies are independent of GCaMP expression levels and transgene expression. When responses occur, rise times are stereotyped across stimuli.
results.evaluation: The characterization of AIA response properties is thorough and well-controlled. Baseline stability (C37), dose-dependence (C38-C40), and independence from technical factors (C45-C46) are clearly demonstrated. The analysis of trial-to-trial variability (C47-C49) appropriately uses paired pulse experiments and correlation analysis. The stereotyped rise times (C50) are shown in supplementary data with appropriate alignment methods. These are important characterization data supporting the main conclusions.

results.result: AWA-defective mutants (odr-7, odr-10) show less reliable AIA responses to high diacetyl concentrations, but retain some residual response. This residual response suggests additional diacetyl-sensing neurons communicate with AIA through chemical synapses, consistent with the wiring diagram showing AIA receives chemical synapses from many chemosensory neurons.
results.evaluation: The reduced reliability in AWA mutants (C51) is clearly shown in Figure 2A-B. The residual response (C75) is evident in the same data. The inference about additional sensory inputs (C76) is logical and supported by the wiring diagram data (C77, Supplementary file 1). This sets up the subsequent experiments identifying glutamatergic inhibition. The logic is sound though the specific identity of additional excitatory inputs is not fully resolved.

results.result: The rapid AIA response to direct optogenetic stimulation indicates that delayed responses to sensory stimuli are not due to slow intrinsic calcium dynamics but rather to circuit-level properties requiring integration of multiple inputs.
results.evaluation: Direct AIA optogenetic stimulation (C67, Figure 2G-H) shows rapid responses, contrasting with delayed responses to AWA stimulation or low-dose odors. This control experiment (C73) appropriately rules out slow intrinsic dynamics as an explanation for delayed sensory responses. The inference about circuit-level delays (C74) is logical and supported by subsequent findings about requirement for multiple inputs. This is an important control supporting the integration model.

results.result: AWA is not the source of ASE's diacetyl response (response preserved in odr-10 mutants), and ASK, AWC, and ASE do not respond to AWA optogenetic stimulation, indicating these sensory neurons detect odors independently rather than through AWA signaling.
results.evaluation: The odr-10 control (C104) appropriately tests whether AWA signals to ASE. The lack of responses to AWA::Chrimson in other sensory neurons (C105) is clearly shown in supplementary data. These controls support the conclusion that sensory neurons detect odors independently, which is important for the model of parallel sensory pathways converging on AIA. The experiments are straightforward and well-controlled.

results.result: E. coli OP50-conditioned medium, which activates AWA and ASE while inhibiting AWC and ASK, elicits reliable AIA responses with similar dynamics to high concentrations of diacetyl or isoamyl alcohol. This demonstrates that the AND-gate logic applies to complex natural food stimuli.
results.evaluation: The OP50 response data (C120) is shown in Figure 5L and supplements. The sensory neuron response profile (C119) is cited from prior work (Zaslaver et al., 2015). The conclusion that AND-gate logic applies to natural stimuli (C121) is supported by the similarity in response dynamics and the engagement of multiple sensory pathways. This extends the findings from defined odors to more naturalistic stimuli, strengthening the biological relevance.

results.result: For both diacetyl and isoamyl alcohol, AIA activation timing matches the arrival of the second sensory input rather than the first. At low odor levels, glutamatergic neuron inhibition is graded and gradual, and AWA action potentials lag stimulus onset by ~1 second, contributing to delayed AIA responses.
results.evaluation: The timing analysis (C133) is shown in supplementary figures with simultaneous recordings of multiple neurons. The graded nature of inhibition (C134) is evident in Figure 5A-C. The AWA action potential timing (C135) is appropriately cited from prior work (Liu et al., 2018). These observations explain the mechanistic basis for delayed AIA responses at low stimulus levels and support the AND-gate model requiring coincident inputs.

results.result: The AIA AND-gate computation is compared to similar mechanisms in other systems: plateau potentials in C. elegans RMD neurons, AND-gates in transcriptional regulation and coincidence detection in neural circuits, mixed chemical-electrical synapses in escape circuits, disinhibition in the inferior olive and mammalian cortex. The authors speculate this combination of features may represent a general circuit motif in C. elegans.
results.evaluation: These claims provide appropriate context by citing relevant literature (C136, C140-C141, C151-C160) comparing the AIA mechanism to similar phenomena in other systems. The comparisons are accurate based on the cited references. The speculation about a general circuit motif (C166) is appropriately qualified as speculative. These contextual claims support the significance of the findings but are primarily literature-based rather than experimental contributions of this study.

results.result: Background information about C. elegans nervous system, chemosensory system, sensory neuron functions, and prior knowledge about AIA's behavioral roles and responses to attractive odors. These establish the context and prior knowledge for the current study.
results.evaluation: These are background claims citing established literature (White et al., 1986; Bargmann, 2006; Robertson and Thomas, 2006; Bargmann et al., 1993; Troemel et al., 1997; Shinkai et al., 2011; Larsch et al., 2013, 2015; Chalasani et al., 2007, 2010; Cho et al., 2016; López-Cruz et al., 2019). The citations appear appropriate and the claims accurately represent prior knowledge. These provide essential context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Comparison of AIA to AIB interneuron: AIB shows less reliable coupling to odor stimuli (57% vs >90% for AIA), integrates sensory input with motor state, and receives equal synaptic input from sensory neurons and interneurons (unlike AIA which receives 3x more from sensory neurons). This may explain why AIA is more coupled to sensory state than AIB.
results.evaluation: The comparison to AIB is based on appropriate citations (Chalasani et al., 2007; Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015; White et al., 1986). The wiring diagram analysis (C147-C148) is cited appropriately. The inference about differential coupling to sensory vs. motor state (C149) is logical based on the connectivity differences, though it is not directly tested in this study. This provides useful context for understanding AIA's specific role.

results.result: Summary statement that AWA excites AIA via electrical synapses in the context of chemical synapses from other neurons, as predicted by the wiring diagram.
results.evaluation: This is an accurate summary of the major findings regarding synaptic mechanisms (supported by claims C3, C4, C56-C66, C78-C93). It correctly notes that the findings match wiring diagram predictions. This summary claim is well-supported by the experimental data.
